#36392. How a green economy could help reverse climate change

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1455 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

How a green economy could help reverse climate change

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1455 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that human civilization is currently profoundly unsustainable.
  • If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.
  • It's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that human civilization is currently profoundly unsustainable. Earth has already crossed seven of the nine planetary boundaries critical for sustaining life, including climate change, ocean acidification and biosphere integrity.

If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.

It's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change. That's where the idea of green growth comes in.

Recent findings suggest that its promise is to keep growing the economy while reducing emissions and resource use. That involves, for instance, running factories, businesses and homes on wind, solar and other green energy instead of coal and gas, replacing gas-fired furnaces with heat pumps and  recycling and reusing resources and raw materials.

According to recent reports, "Basically, the idea is: business as usual, but with more sustainable technologies," remarked Helmut Haberl, a social ecology professor at BOKU University in Vienna. Along with his colleagues, he published a major report in 2020 evaluating more than 800 studies on green growth.

Sources indicate that in principle, the world's economic output could continue to grow in the long term and generate significantly fewer emissions from the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. That's been shown in scenarios modeled by researchers with the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC.

Thanks to renewable energy and green technologies, those scenarios have already become reality in several countries and regions.

According to recent reports, the economies of developed countries like the United Kingdom, the United States, Japanand Australia have experienced years of growth alongside sinking CO2 emissions. That's even when offshore production is included.

Sources indicate that in the European Union, the bloc-wide economy has grown by more than 70% since 1990. Meanwhile, the EU's carbon emissions have dropped by around 40%.

But such a complete decoupling of growth and emissions is, according to Haberl and his fellow researchers, relatively rare.

Recent findings suggest that in India, and in several countries in Africa and Southeast Asia, economies are becoming more efficient. But while economic performance is outpacing emissions growth, emissions are still rising in those countries and globally. This is not compatible with preventing the worst impacts of climate change.

"That doesn't mean, however, that it couldn't work in the future," said Haberl, referring to decoupling of growth and emissions.

And even though economic growth has been shown to be compatible with emissions reduction, eliminating all greenhouse gases from a polluting industry like steel or chemicals is complicated.

These sectors don't just release emissions by burning fossil fuels for energy; carbon is also a key part of the chemical processes used to create their products, notably in the steel industry.

Replacing it with greener substitutes, or an alternative energy source like green hydrogen, requires significant investment.

There's another hurdle: the world's high consumption of resources. A productive economy depends on many raw materials and other products: ores, chemicals, wood, cement, glass and agricultural products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Many countries are now using green technologies to reduce the amount of resources needed to manufacture a product, for example, and are making their economies more efficient.

But that doesn't mean overall fewer resources are being used because falling costs can encourage businesses to produce more things and people to consume more. This can partially offset green savings and is called the rebound effect.

The British economy has been growing for years, emissions have been dropping and efficiency has increased, but the UK still used 7% more resources in 2023 than it did in 2001.

In a recent development, global resource consumption has tripled over the last 50 years. If the world continues on the current pathway, that could increase by another 60% by 2060. It remains unclear whether green growth can deliver the emissions and resource reductions needed to stop climate change and biodiversity loss rapidly enough.

"We really need to move beyond efficiency gains in our existing production practices to look more broadly at what we consume," said Catherine Ganzleben, a sustainability and fair transitions expert at the European Environment Agency.

She told DW that people also need to reconsider how they consume and whether they really need to own everything they use in their daily life — cars, for example.

"But we can shift towards models where we share cars, so we pool our resources and have significantly lower resources per person through sharing the goods that we need.".

Some researchers have concluded that unrestricted economic growth is no longer possible in the long term, even if it's sustainable.

Instead, they've called for degrowth. This posits slower economic growth, no growth at all or even negative growth, so that the world's ecosystems and the climate have a chance to recover and stabilize.

It has been revealed that that applies mainly to economies in richer countries, which would need to take targeted steps to reduce their energy and resource use. Poorer countries would continue to grow until their economies and quality of life improve significantly.

Recent findings suggest that under the degrowth theory, a society's prosperity is not measured solely by the growth of its gross domestic product, but by values such as quality of life, education and community. The idea is that once countries develop to a certain point, additional growth doesn't translate into greater well-being.

In a recent development, ultimately, the concept is based on the idea that human well-being and ecological sustainability is only possible in the long term with a planned, socially just reduction of material production and resource consumption. Degrowth advocates argue this would be preferable to an unplanned and potentially catastrophic economic contraction caused by escalating climate extremes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A 2020 study by researchers from the universities of Leeds and Lausanne highlighted that the concept of degrowth supported the world's climate goals — and that a high quality of life didn't have to be sacrificed in exchange for a significantly lower consumption of energy and resources.

However, there is still no conclusive evidence that an entire modern economy could continue to function entirely on the degrowth principles in the long term.

Nevertheless, Haberl doesn't assume that an environmentally friendly economic model automatically goes hand in hand with sacrifice, arguing instead for a needs-based economy.

According to recent reports, "A society isn't necessarily better off when it's producing more goods and services," he said. It all depends on how prosperity and quality of life are measured in the future, and how states decide to do business.

Today, a successful economy is measured by the growth of a country's gross domestic product — put simply, the worth of all of its goods and services. This calculation doesn't account for income distribution, unpaid work, quality of life or environmental damage.

Recent findings suggest that "The highest possible real incomes for every individual would probably not be compatible with ecological goals in the long term," said Haberl. "On the other hand, an increase in prosperity — related to a higher quality of life — would be.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, an analysis by the European Environment Agency (EEA) pointed out that the idea of steady growth is part of the world's economic cycle, and deeply anchored in our institutions, norms and societal discourse. The job market and tax system are also closely tied to gross domestic product growth. A shrinking economy would therefore require a fundamental shift in our way of thinking.

Industry observers note that countries face a dilemma: a steadily growing economy is not compatible with ecological goals, according to the EEA. On the other side, a sharp decline in growth could trigger enormous social upheaval.

In a recent development, and the correlation is much more complex than the idea of "less is more," as highlighted by an EEA study in November 2021. "The fact that GDP growth has been harmful for the environment does not necessarily mean that declining GDP would be good for the environment," noted the report.

Sources indicate that achieving green growth while respecting environmental limits would require an "unprecedented decoupling of economic activity from environmental and climate pressures. Whether this is feasible is presently uncertain.".

Feds arrest top official of healthcare organization, alleging illegal drug importation

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • authorities are accusing the two top officials of a Canadian company of operating a long-running scheme to illegally import prescription drugs into the U.S., according to court records filed Tuesday.
  • John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the manufacturer, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges, according to the records.
  • Bob Howard, his brother, who is president and a director of CANARX, is also wanted in the federal investigation, according to an affidavit from Dustin Dobbs, a special agent with the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Criminal Investigations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

U.S. authorities are accusing the two top officials of a Canadian company of operating a long-running scheme to illegally import prescription drugs into the U.S., according to court records filed Tuesday.

John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the manufacturer, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges, according to the records.

Bob Howard, his brother, who is president and a director of CANARX, is also wanted in the federal investigation, according to an affidavit from Dustin Dobbs, a special agent with the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Criminal Investigations. He has not yet been taken into custody.

Besides conspiracy and smuggling, the arrest warrant noted John Thomas Howard was charged with introducing misbranded drugs into interstate commerce and illegal drug importation. No plea has been filed.

CANARX was featured in a CNBC investigation last year that revealed how the company and others known as alternative funding programs, or AFPs, are becoming more pervasive around the U.S. as drug costs skyrocket. The investigation found these companies have penetrated the country's healthcare system by offering high-cost specialty drugs at more affordable prices through private and public employers. In some cases, employers are requiring their staff to use an AFP.

Recent findings suggest that AFPs often obtain the medications overseas and ship them directly to patients, a practice that federal authorities have said is illegal and poses safety risks. CNBC traced the trail of drugs from abroad to the U.S. via a supply chain that the pharmaceutical companies producing the medications have not authorized.

On its website, CANARX, founded in 2002 and based in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, described its business as the first international prescription provider for the U.S. and the safest such program in the industry. The company noted it sources its medications from Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and Newly introduced Zealand.

But the affidavit said that the FDA's investigation found "there is probable cause to believe that (CANARX) illegally imported or caused the illegal importation of prescription drugs into the United States ….".

According to recent reports, the affidavit does not specify which medications the agency believes were illegally imported. The criminal complaint covers the period from Feb. 22, 2017, through April 15, 2026.

The company's general counsel, Joseph Morris, told CNBC in a statement: "The Howards deny all the charges against them, will defend vigorously, and expect to be vindicated in court.".

In a recent development, the company has been under FDA scrutiny for several years. In 2023, the agency seized medication being shipped by CANARX that it says was potentially misbranded and counterfeit, according to an email sent to a patient that was obtained by CNBC.

And in 2019, the FDA sent a warning letter to the tech giant, saying it was operating "in a manner that substitutes the FDA-approved drugs prescribed by the U.S. healthcare provider with unapproved drugs." Morris, in response to that warning, argued CANARX was not misleading patients, but agreed for the company to stop importing drugs that need to be administered by a doctor.

In an interview as part of the CNBC investigation, Morris said last year that the medicines shipped to U.S. patients come from highly regulated countries. He said CANARX was operating legally.

The central question for AFPs is the legality of importing prescription drugs into the U.S. for personal use. The FDA allows Americans to import medications for individual use in some cases if the drug is not available domestically. That is the basis on which the AFPs built their models for shipping medicines directly to patients.

But an FDA spokesperson told CNBC last year that "in most circumstances, a person cannot import prescription drugs from other countries into the U.S. ... as substitutes for FDA-approved drugs.".

In a separate civil lawsuit that is pending, Gilead Sciences accused CANARX and other companies of illegally importing Biktarvy, its medication to treat HIV.

Sources indicate that in a statement to CNBC on Wednesday, a Gilead spokesperson remarked the company "has taken strong legal action to protect patients and the integrity of the U.S. medicines supply chain. We welcome the government's efforts to hold accountable those whose conduct may put patients at risk.".

CANARX has not responded to the Gilead lawsuit.

— CNBC's Paige Tortorelli and Melissa Lee contributed to this report.

#36388. Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1218 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that why do some volcanoes send towering fountains of lava into the sky while others release molten rock in much calmer eruptions?
  • In a recent development, an international research team led by The University of Manchester investigated volcanic material from the 2021 Tajogaite eruption on La Palma, Spain.
  • Superheating occurs when magma reaches temperatures above those at which its crystals would normally remain stable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that why do some volcanoes send towering fountains of lava into the sky while others release molten rock in much calmer eruptions? Scientists have discovered that a hidden effect of extreme heat inside magma may help explain these striking differences.

In a recent development, an international research team led by The University of Manchester investigated volcanic material from the 2021 Tajogaite eruption on La Palma, Spain. Their findings reveal that a process known as "superheating" can dramatically slow the formation of crystals inside magma as it travels upward toward Earth's surface.

Superheating occurs when magma reaches temperatures above those at which its crystals would normally remain stable. The researchers found that this extra heat can keep magma relatively fluid for much longer than expected, potentially allowing it to rise rapidly and produce spectacular lava fountains.

The discovery, published in Nature Communications, offers new insight into a long-standing question in volcanology: How does magma's temperature history influence the way a volcano erupts?

How Extreme Heat Changes Magma Deep Inside Volcanoes.

Magma is a mixture of molten rock, gases, and sometimes solid crystals beneath Earth's surface. Once it emerges from a volcano, it is called lava. Although temperature and chemical composition are key in determining how magma behaves, the upcoming research suggests that the heating it experienced before an eruption can also make a major difference.

Under normal conditions, crystals begin forming as magma cools. This process often starts around tiny existing crystals that act as "seeds," providing surfaces on which additional crystals can grow.

Superheating can disrupt this process in two crucial ways. First, sufficiently high temperatures can dissolve the microscopic crystal seeds that would otherwise encourage latest crystals to develop. Second, the heat changes the internal structure of the molten material, making it more uniform and less favorable for new crystal formation.

Sources indicate that these changes matter because crystals affect magma's viscosity, which describes how easily a substance flows. As more crystals develop, magma generally becomes thicker and more resistant to movement. This can influence both its speed of ascent and the way trapped volcanic gases escape.

Lead author Dr. Barbara Bonechi, Research Associate at The University of Manchester, explained:.

"The history of crystal and bubble growth can dramatically control how a magma erupts, in particular as more crystals grow, they eventually have a dramatic effect on magma viscosity. Until now, we did not fully understand the dynamics of crystal growth for magmas that received an injection of superheat just before ascent. But using our exciting and newly developed X-ray transparent pressure vessel combined with synchrotron X-ray microtomography, we can actually observe these processes 'in situ'.".

Scientists Discover an Eight-Hour Delay in Crystal Formation.

Sources indicate that to investigate what happens inside superheated magma, the researchers recreated volcanic conditions in the laboratory using material collected from the Tajogaite eruption. The magma involved in that eruption may have experienced superheating before reaching the surface and while rising through Earth's crust.

The team conducted experiments under carefully controlled temperatures and pressures designed to reproduce conditions encountered by magma underground.

Recent findings suggest that at Diamond Light Source, a major scientific research facility, the researchers used synchrotron X-ray microtomography to watch crystals develop in real time. This advanced imaging technique uses extremely powerful X-rays to examine the internal structure of materials in three dimensions without having to cut them open.

A specially developed pressure vessel that allows X-rays to pass through it made these observations possible while the magma was subjected to volcanic conditions.

The team also performed complementary experiments in Prague, where samples could be examined over longer periods outside the real-time imaging setup. Together, these approaches allowed the researchers to observe how different heating conditions affected the timing of crystal formation.

The results revealed a remarkable difference.

Magma that had not undergone superheating began producing crystals after approximately 20 minutes. However, when magma was subjected to strong superheating, the beginning of crystallization was delayed for more than eight hours.

This substantial delay suggests that intense heating can leave magma without newly forming crystals for far longer than scientists might otherwise expect, with potentially notable consequences for volcanic eruptions.

Why Superheated Magma Could Produce Towering Lava Fountains.

The researchers next explored how these laboratory findings might affect real volcanoes.

According to recent reports, they incorporated the measured delays in crystal formation into computer models that simulate how magma rises through Earth's crust. These models account for changes in magma properties as the molten material moves toward the surface.

The simulations revealed two very different possibilities.

When superheating delays crystallization, magma can remain relatively fluid as it rises. Because it encounters less resistance to flowing, it may travel upward more rapidly, potentially creating conditions that favor dramatic lava fountains.

These spectacular eruptions occur when escaping volcanic gases propel molten rock high above a vent, producing jets and fountains of glowing lava.

It has been revealed that in contrast, magma that begins crystallizing earlier becomes more viscous and tends to ascend more slowly. This slower movement gives volcanic gases additional time to escape, favoring gentler eruptions in which lava flows out onto the surface rather than being thrown high into the air.

Such behavior is known as an effusive eruption, a type of volcanic activity characterized primarily by flowing lava.

The findings suggest that even when volcanic systems have similar characteristics, differences in their earlier heating histories may help explain why their eruptions look and behave so differently.

A New Clue for Predicting Volcanic Eruptions.

Industry observers note that understanding what happens to magma before it reaches the surface is essential for assessing volcanic hazards. Scientists monitor signals such as earthquakes, ground deformation, and volcanic gas emissions to identify changes within active volcanoes.

However, predicting exactly how an eruption will unfold remains difficult. Two volcanoes with seemingly similar magma compositions and gas conditions can still display markedly different eruptive behavior.

The newly introduced research suggests that the effects of superheating and the timing of crystal formation deserve greater attention in volcanic forecasting models.

By accounting for these previously underappreciated processes, researchers may eventually be able to better interpret volcanic monitoring data and assess whether rising magma is more likely to produce vigorous lava fountains or gentler lava flows.

In a recent development, the results do not mean that magma temperature alone determines how explosive an eruption will be. Instead, they identify another important piece of the complex physical processes that shape volcanic activity.

Co-author Dr. Margherita Polacci, Senior Lecturer in Volcanology at The University of Manchester, highlighted the potential importance of the findings for understanding volcanic hazards:.

Recent findings suggest that "Current volcanic hazard models typically focus on magma chemistry, gas content and pressure changes. This work suggests that pre-eruptive thermal history and crystallization kinetics may also play an crucial role in controlling magma ascent and eruptive behavior, with implications for volcanic hazard assessment.".

Materials provided by University of Manchester. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
